title: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN): A Framework for Overlaying Virtualized Layer 2 Networks over Layer 3 Networks
summary: This document describes VXLAN, a scheme for building overlay networks that carry virtualized Layer 2 networks over Layer 3 networks. It addresses multi-tenant needs in cloud and enterprise data centers, and documents the deployed protocol for the Internet community.

plainLanguage.summary: It is like building many separate virtual neighborhoods on top of one big road network, so each customer thinks they have their own street. VXLAN does this by putting their traffic in special envelopes.

questions: what is a vni in vxlan
what udp port does vxlan use
subtitle: Wrapping Ethernet frames in UDP so virtual machines can share one Layer 2 network across a Layer 3 data center.

tldr.problem: Virtualized, multi-tenant data centers strain the 4094 VLAN limit, the MAC address tables of top-of-rack switches, and Spanning Tree, yet VMs still need a Layer 2 model across the whole network.
tldr.mechanism: VXLAN wraps each VM's Ethernet frame in an outer Ethernet, IP, UDP and 8-byte VXLAN header. A 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) marks the segment, and tunnel end points (VTEPs) add and remove the wrapper.
tldr.outcome: Up to 16 M segments can coexist, tenants can reuse MAC addresses safely, and the VM never sees the encapsulation. The RFC documents a protocol that was already deployed.

today: RFC 7348 is an Informational RFC published through the Independent Submission stream. The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC itself says it documents the deployed VXLAN protocol for the benefit of the Internet community.

sections.title: The Data Center Problem
sections.content:
Server virtualization means a physical server hosts many virtual machines (VMs), each with its own MAC address. The RFC lists three pressures. First, Spanning Tree blocks links to prevent loops, so operators pay for ports and links they cannot use, and a 12-bit VLAN ID limits a network to fewer than 4094 VLANs.

Second, multi-tenant clouds need isolated networks for many customers on shared infrastructure, and tenants may independently pick the same MAC addresses, VLAN IDs or Layer 3 addresses. Third, top-of-rack (ToR) switches must now learn the MAC addresses of individual VMs, which could be hundreds per server. If the table overflows, the switch may stop learning new addresses until idle entries age out, leading to significant flooding.
sections.plainLanguage: A big building where many families live needs a separate hallway for each family, but there are only so many hallways, and the doorman cannot remember every person's name.

sections.title: How VXLAN Works
sections.content:
VXLAN is a Layer 2 overlay scheme on a Layer 3 network. Each overlay is a VXLAN segment identified by a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI), which allows up to 16 M segments in one administrative domain. Only VMs in the same segment can talk, and the VNI lets segments have overlapping MAC addresses without traffic crossing over.

The VXLAN Tunnel End Point (VTEP) sits, for example, in the hypervisor. When a VM sends a frame, the VTEP looks up the VNI, finds the remote VTEP for the destination MAC, and prepends an outer MAC, outer IP header and VXLAN header. The remote VTEP checks the VNI, strips the headers and hands the frame to the VM. The VMs never see any of this. The tunnels are stateless.

The remote VTEP also learns the mapping from the inner source MAC to the outer source IP, so replies need no flooding. This document focuses on this data plane learning scheme as the control plane, and notes that central directory-based push or pull schemes are also possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The delivery person at your building puts your letter in a bigger envelope marked with your neighborhood number. At the other building, another delivery person opens the big envelope and hands you the original letter.

sections.title: Broadcast and Multicast Handling
sections.content:
A VM looking for another VM sends an ARP broadcast. With VXLAN, the broadcast is encapsulated and sent to the IP multicast group that the segment uses. A mapping between each VNI and its multicast group is made at the management layer and given to the VTEPs, which use IGMP membership reports to join and leave the groups.

The VTEP uses (*,G) joins, because the set of tunnel sources is unknown and changes often. Because each VTEP can be both source and destination, the RFC notes bidirectional PIM would be more efficient. Multicast frames and unknown-destination frames travel the same multicast tree. The destination VM answers the ARP with a unicast reply, which is encapsulated back to the originating VTEP using the learned mapping.

VXLAN can also run over a Layer 2 physical network, where IGMP snooping helps replicate multicast efficiently. VTEPs MUST NOT fragment VXLAN packets. The RFC recommends that MTUs across the physical network be set to accommodate the larger encapsulated frame, and says Path MTU discovery may also be used.
sections.plainLanguage: If you shout "who lives here?", VXLAN sends the shout only to the right neighborhood group. The one who answers replies straight back to you.

sections.title: The VXLAN Frame Format
sections.content:
Reading from the inside out, the original Ethernet frame (without its FCS) is wrapped in four headers. The VXLAN header is 8 bytes: an 8-bit flags field, where the I flag MUST be 1 for a valid VNI and the other seven bits are reserved, a 24-bit VNI, and reserved fields of 24 bits and 8 bits that MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The outer UDP header uses destination port 4789, assigned by IANA, which SHOULD be the default and be configurable because some early implementations used other values. The source port is recommended to be a hash of fields from the inner packet, in the range 49152-65535, so ECMP load balancing can spread traffic. The UDP checksum SHOULD be sent as zero, and a receiver MUST accept a zero checksum for decapsulation. A non-zero checksum, if included, must be correct, and a receiver that verifies it and fails MUST drop the packet.

The outer IP header carries the source VTEP address and a unicast or multicast destination. The outer Ethernet header has an optional VLAN tag. The frame can be carried over either IPv4 or IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The special envelope has a label with your neighborhood number, a stamp saying which post office door to use, and the return and delivery addresses of the two delivery people.

sections.title: Deployment and Gateways
sections.content:
In the RFC's example, two servers each run a hypervisor VTEP across a Layer 3 network, and VMs on VNIs 22, 34, 74 and 98 reach their peers on the other server. A tunnel end point can also be a physical server or switch, in hardware or software.

A VXLAN gateway forwards between VXLAN and non-VXLAN (for example VLAN-based) networks. Incoming VXLAN frames are decapsulated and forwarded by inner destination MAC. In the other direction, frames are mapped to a VNI from their VLAN ID. Gateways can be ToR switches, core devices or even WAN edge routers.

For inner VLAN tags, decapsulated frames with an inner VLAN tag SHOULD be discarded unless configured otherwise. A VTEP SHOULD NOT include an inner VLAN tag, and SHOULD strip one from a frame it encapsulates, unless configured otherwise.
sections.plainLanguage: A gateway is a door between a VXLAN neighborhood and the ordinary streets, swapping envelopes for plain letters as things go through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Carrying Layer 2 over IP widens the attack surface. Rogues could join the multicast groups that carry a segment's broadcast traffic, or inject MAC-over-UDP frames to inject spurious traffic or hijack MAC addresses. The RFC says VXLAN itself includes no specific measures against these attacks and relies on traditional mechanisms layered on IP.

It sketches options: limit who can deploy VMs and gateways, use 802.1X for admission control, use 5-tuple ACLs on physical switches (made possible by the UDP encapsulation), and secure tunneled traffic with IPsec, which needs an authentication infrastructure. It also recommends designating a VLAN for VXLAN traffic and communicating VNI and VM membership mappings over existing secure methods.
sections.plainLanguage: Since the envelopes travel on shared roads, a sneaky person could drop fake envelopes in. The RFC suggests locks and guards, such as IPsec, instead of building them in.
